clue.text: One tending to flap like wings with water vapour on

parts.note: alar is an adjective meaning of or like wings
mist is water vapour hanging in the air

explanation.surface: A nervous bird beats its wings as the steam rises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flap' is the noun sense, a panic, not the beating of wings the surface suggests; 'on' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in a flap is to panic, and a scaremonger is someone given to spreading panic.

clue.text: Composition in A, perhaps

explanation.surface: A piece of writing is filed under the letter A.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A' is the indefinite article in grammar; a composition is also a written piece in a newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: A piece written for a newspaper is a composition; in grammar, 'a' is the indefinite one of these parts of speech.

clue.text: As excellent as Barrie's butler

parts.note: J M Barrie wrote a play about a resourceful butler whose title calls him excellent

explanation.surface: Someone is praised as being as fine as the famous butler in a Barrie play.
explanation.walkthrough: J M Barrie's play 'The Admirable Crichton' is about a butler who takes charge when the family is shipwrecked.
explanation.definitionFit: Barrie's play title gives the butler Crichton this epithet, meaning worthy of praise or excellent.

clue.text: Badly aimed shots fail to hit lines, we hear

indicators.note: we hear tells us the words are judged by how they sound when spoken

parts.note: fail to hit is miss, and lines of waiting people are queues

explanation.surface: Wayward shots miss the lines, so people say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we hear' turns MISS plus QUEUES into a word of the same sound; the shots are snooker or billiard strokes.
explanation.definitionFit: A bad stroke in billiards or snooker where the cue fails to strike the ball properly is a poorly aimed shot.

clue.text: In this event, your number's up!

definitions.text: In this event, your number's up!

indicators.note: In says the letters sit inside the run of words this event, your, read straight through

explanation.surface: A warning that this occasion marks the end for you.
explanation.walkthrough: Psalm 90 gives the human lifespan as threescore years and ten, so at that age your number is up; the run of letters spans three words.
explanation.definitionFit: Threescore and ten is the traditional allotted span of human life, after which one's time is up.

clue.text: Language often modified or changed a lot

indicators.note: changed tells us the letters of these words are put in a new order

parts.note: a lot means many

explanation.surface: A tongue that keeps shifting has altered a great deal.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gypsy tongue survives in many local mixed forms, so it is a language often modified.

clue.text: Remove from Exeter say, and go to the country

explanation.surface: Someone is sent down from Exeter and heads off into the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: To rusticate a student is to suspend them from a university such as Exeter; it also means to retire to rural life.
explanation.definitionFit: Rustication is temporary suspension from college; the verb also means to move to rural parts, from Latin rus, countryside.

clue.text: Noble married relation

parts.note: an agnate is a relative on the father's side

explanation.surface: A nobleman wed a relative.
explanation.definitionFit: A magnate is a great and powerful person, historically a nobleman of high rank.

clue.text: Two presents not located

parts.note: the present time is now
being present means being here

explanation.surface: A pair of gifts has gone missing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'presents' looks like gifts, but it gives two senses of 'present': the present moment and being present.
explanation.definitionFit: Something with no place at all is not to be found anywhere, so it is not located.

clue.text: Paper declares these are short cuts

parts.note: The Times is a British newspaper
to aver is to declare firmly

explanation.surface: A newspaper announces some quick routes.
explanation.definitionFit: Short cuts save minutes, so they are devices for saving time.

clue.text: Advice to young man to get new garment for girl

parts.note: 'Go west, young man' was famous advice; west is abbreviated to W

explanation.surface: A young man is told to go and buy a new dress for his girlfriend.
explanation.walkthrough: The advice is the old American saying 'Go west, young man', written GO W with W for west.
explanation.definitionFit: A long formal dress is a typical woman's garment for an evening out.

clue.text: Achieve success as all-rounder, in the main

definitions.text: Achieve success as all-rounder, in the main

parts.words: Achieve success as all-rounder, in the main
parts.note: a sporting all-rounder is reread as someone who goes all round the world on the main, the sea

explanation.surface: A cricketer excels with bat and ball, mostly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the main' looks like 'mostly', but here 'the main' is the open sea, and an all-rounder is a sailor going right round the globe.
explanation.definitionFit: To sail all the way round the globe is the voyage that makes a seafarer an all-rounder.

clue.text: Mission maybe involved capturing vessel

indicators.note: capturing means the scrambled letters hold the vessel inside them
involved means twisted up, so the letters of maybe are scrambled

parts.note: SS stands for steamship, a vessel

explanation.surface: A mission was perhaps part of seizing a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mission' looks like a task, but it is a diplomatic one; 'involved' turns the letters of the word maybe into EMBAY.
explanation.definitionFit: A diplomatic mission is the body of envoys based in a foreign capital, housed in a legation.

clue.text: Ask for midshipman's views in drinking-place?

definitions.text: Ask for midshipman's views in drinking-place?

parts.words: Ask for midshipman's views in drinking-place?
parts.note: Captain Marryat's novel hero is Mr Midshipman Easy, so asking for his views is telling him to talk

explanation.surface: Someone seeks a naval cadet's opinion in a bar.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Midshipman Easy is the hero of Captain Marryat's novel; 'Speak, Easy!' invites him to give his views, and an illicit Prohibition-era bar bears the name.
explanation.definitionFit: An illegal bar during American Prohibition was a drinking-place where patrons were told to keep their voices low.

clue.text: Fellows in political faction such primitive types?

parts.note: a cave is a breakaway political group, after the Cave of Adullam in British parliamentary history
fellows means men

explanation.surface: Are the members of a splinter group of politicians really so primitive?
explanation.walkthrough: A 'cave' is a historical British term for a group of MPs who break from their party; men in a cave are the primitive types.
explanation.definitionFit: Prehistoric people who sheltered in rock dwellings stand for crude, primitive types.

clue.text: Successful sportsman still made blunders

indicators.note: blunders suggests the letters of these words are muddled into a fresh order

explanation.surface: A winning athlete nevertheless made mistakes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blunders' looks like the verb of the surface, but it is the anagram signal on STILL MADE.
explanation.definitionFit: A sportsman who wins a place on the podium is awarded gold, silver or bronze, so is successful.

clue.text: Notice the sulphur is boiling

parts.note: to notice is to see
taken as written
S is the chemical symbol for sulphur

explanation.surface: Look: the sulphur in the flask is bubbling away.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that bubbles and churns while heated is boiling, as a liquid does.

clue.text: Sculptor setting record with novelist

parts.note: EP is an extended-play record
Gertrude Stein was an American novelist and writer

explanation.surface: An artist puts a disc on with a writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Jacob Epstein was a famous American-born British sculptor of the twentieth century.

clue.text: Judged, however, before start of tribunal

parts.note: though can mean however

indicators.note: start of picks out only the opening letter of the word tribunal

explanation.surface: A verdict is reached, though only before the tribunal begins.
explanation.definitionFit: To have thought something is to have judged or considered it to be so.

clue.text: Went back, restored to former owner

explanation.surface: Someone retreated and handed property back to its previous holder.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is a pun: to cede is to hand over, so re-ceded means handed back again.
explanation.definitionFit: Went back means withdrew, as a tide does; ceded again means given back to the one who held it before.

clue.text: Guillotine to cause terror? Correct

indicators.note: a guillotine cuts off the head, so the first letter of the word is removed

parts.note: to frighten is to cause terror

explanation.surface: Was the guillotine meant to spread fear? That is right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guillotine' beheads FRIGHTEN, removing its F.
explanation.definitionFit: To put something right or straighten it out is to correct it.

clue.text: Sort of bridge hand to produce tricks

explanation.surface: A kind of bridge deal designed for taking tricks.
explanation.walkthrough: In bridge a chicane is a hand with no trumps; as a verb it means to use trickery.
explanation.definitionFit: A bridge deal holding no trump card has this name; the verb means deceive by trickery or quibbling.

clue.text: Archaic imprisonment for French tributary

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned jail term is handed out for a French river.
explanation.walkthrough: The Durance is a river in south-east France feeding the Rhône; 'durance vile' is an old phrase for imprisonment.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for confinement in prison; also the river in Provence that flows into the Rhône.

clue.text: Fatted calf as Christmas present?

parts.note: a fattened calf is livestock that has been filled out, punning on a small gift put in a Christmas sock

explanation.surface: Someone gives a fattened calf as a festive gift.
explanation.walkthrough: Livestock is 'stock', and a calf fed up is a stock filler, punning on the small gifts placed in a Christmas sock.
explanation.definitionFit: A small gift tucked into a hung-up Christmas sock is the usual festive present of that name.

clue.text: Composer looked up to in South Africa

definitions.text: looked up to in South Africa

explanation.surface: A composer was much admired in South Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: Alban Berg was an Austrian composer; in South Africa a berg is a mountain, literally something you look up to.
explanation.definitionFit: Alban Berg wrote the opera Wozzeck; in Afrikaans usage the word means a mountain, which people gaze upward at.

clue.text: Saturnalia unusual for a Victorian, say

indicators.note: unusual tells us the letters of the word are set out in an odd new order

explanation.surface: A Victorian-era person would have found the Roman winter festival odd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Victorian' looks like the 19th-century era, but it means someone from the Australian state of Victoria.
explanation.definitionFit: Victoria is a state of Australia, so a Victorian is one example of a person from that country.

clue.text: Not, so to speak, leading to easy conclusion?

definitions.text: Not, so to speak, leading to easy conclusion?

parts.words: Not, so to speak, leading to easy conclusion?
parts.note: the word not said aloud sounds like a tangle of rope, and a tangled problem does not lead to an easy conclusion

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a negative leads to a simple ending.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue says 'not' aloud as KNOT, then describes a problem full of knots that cannot be easily resolved.
explanation.definitionFit: A tangled, intricate problem is hard to solve and does not lead to an easy answer.

clue.text: Upset a French piece of furniture

parts.note: un is French for a
a settle is a high-backed wooden bench

explanation.surface: Someone knocks over a piece of French furniture.
explanation.walkthrough: A settle is a long wooden bench with a high back, common in old British farmhouses and inns.
explanation.definitionFit: To upset someone is to disturb their composure and throw them off balance.
